newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council authorizes Bosnia force for 18 months.
newsitem.headline: UN Council authorizes Bosnia force for 18 months.

text.p: By a unanimous vote, the Security Council late on Thursday authorised deployment of a NATO-led force in Bosnia for another 18 months, an effort to prevent outbreaks of violence in the Balkan state.
In addition to the troops, the council in a 35-point resolution authorised U.N. civilian operations for 12 months, including an international police force.

Although no U.N. troops are part of the operation, all countries involved sought the approval of the 15-member council to keep a 25,000 to 30,000 peacekeeping force in Bosnia, about half the numbers currently fielded by more than 30 states.
The resolution changes the name of current peace Implementation Force, known as IFOR, to Stabilisation Force or SFOR. The IFOR mandate expires on Dec. 20.

SFOR is being deployed because, while IFOR succeeded in halting the fighting in Bosnia, the political provisions of the November 1995 Dayton accord aimed at knitting back the divided country remain far from being implemented.
This has raised fears of a new outbreak of fighting if IFOR were withdrawn without being replaced by a follow-up military presence.

The resolution also emphasises reconstruction and other civilian tasks, prompting Bosnia's U.N. envoy Muhamed Sacirbey to say: "Our country is in such need of rebuilding that any unkept promise in both pragmatically and symbolically painful."

But he said progress was questionable on a re-integration of the country. "We cannot substitute superficiality for substance, and, that would be exactly the case if more effort was not exerted to insure freedom of movement, freedom of the media, respect for human rights and most critically, the return of refugees and displace persons to their homes."
"A house with a roof but without walls or foundation is either a mirage or a moment of suspended animation just before collapse," he added.

The council is its 35-point resolution also stressed that all states were obliged to cooperate with the U.N. war crimes court, based in the Hague" and "surrender for trial of all persons indicted by the tribunal." Sacirbey said he feared that the tribunal was becoming "marginalized."
IFOR, under instructions to detain only suspects who fall into its hands, has not carried out any arrests and U.S. officials have given no indication that soldiers under SFOR will behave otherwise.

But Russia, which sypathizes with the Serbs, warned that the tribunal could not be used for political purposes. The real aim of the resolution, said Ambassador Sergei Lavrov, was to pursue peace "unil peace becaomes irreversible."
The SFOR operation includes troops from a number of non-NATO countries, including Russia.
The United States, had more than 20,000 troops in IFOR but will now cut down its soldier to 8,000 but still command the operation.

Germany for the first time will field combat soldiers in a Franco-German brigade. Bonn's role in any peacekeeping force has been controversial, both in domestically and internationally, particularly in view of the brutal Nazi occupation of the Balkans in the Second World War.

Thursday's resolution permits the use of force under Chapter VII of the U.N. charter and says the peacekeepers can "take all necessary measures to ensure compliance with the rules and procedures, to be established by the commander of SFOR." This includes control of airspace over Bosnia and all civilian and military air traffic.

And in an apparent reference to American weapons shipped to Bosnians, the council underlined the importance of "control of armaments in the region at the lowest possible level" and said all parties were obligated to pursue arms control agreements they had signed previously.
